reason: The text depicts Balak, king of Moab, as an active leader directing his people against an external threat (Israel). The elders and princes of Moab are shown as loyal servants and messengers carrying out Balak's orders to hire Bilaam the prophet. They travel to Bilaam, deliver his messages, and report back—following his directives without resistance. The antagonism in the passage is directed outward toward Israel (whom Moab fears) and later toward Bilaam (for blessing Israel instead of cursing it), but there is no evidence of internal antagonism between Balak and his own people.
